[Burning of the Khāṇḍava Forest. Chapter 227. 228.] || The Book of Beginnings ||

Arjuna, burning with indignation, repelled the rain with his arrows. Seeing his downpour being rendered ineffective, <term>Śatakratu</term> <gloss>Indra, he of a hundred sacrifices</gloss> increased the rain even more. <term>Pākaśāsana</term> <gloss>Indra, the slayer of the demon Pāka</gloss> created a storm with his high-velocity arrows, causing destruction while delighting the others. <margin>828</margin> <margin>Pāya</margin> Then, lifting a great peak of Mount Mandara with his hands, he hurled it, together with its trees, toward the son of Pāṇḍu, wishing to kill him. Arjuna, with his rapid and flaming-tipped arrows, shattered the mountain peak into a thousand pieces. As the mountain was being destroyed, its form appeared like the sky breaking apart along with the sun, moon, and planets. By that great mountain peak falling down, many creatures residing in the Khāṇḍava forest were struck and killed.
Thus ends the two-hundred and twenty-seventh chapter, the conflict between the gods, Kṛṣṇa, and Arjuna, in the Khāṇḍavadahana section of the Ādiparva. 227.

|| <term>Vaiśampāyana</term> <gloss>a sage and narrator</gloss> said || Terrified by the falling of the mountain, the residents of Khāṇḍava—the <term>Dānavas</term> <gloss>demons</gloss>, <term>Rākṣasas</term> <gloss>ogres</gloss>, <term>Nāgas</term> <gloss>serpents</gloss>, trees, and forest-dwellers—as well as elephants with flowing ichor, tigers, and maned lions, were all deeply agitated and abandoned their homes. <margin>829</margin> They looked upon that forest, angry and with weapons raised, while the ground seemed to move due to the sound of the uprooting. Observing the forest burning on all sides, and seeing Kṛṣṇa with his weapons raised, they let out a terrible roar. Because of that fierce sound and the roar of the fire, the entire sky resounded, as if filled with storm clouds. Then, the long-armed <term>Keśava</term> <gloss>Kṛṣṇa</gloss> released his most fierce, radiant discus to destroy them. <margin>830</margin> Struck by it, the lesser creatures, along with the <term>Dānavas</term> and <term>Niśācaras</term> <gloss>night-wanderers</gloss>, were cut to pieces by the hundreds and fell into the fire in an instant. Those <term>Daityas</term> <gloss>demons</gloss>, torn apart by Kṛṣṇa’s discus and covered in fat and blood, appeared like clouds during twilight. The <term>Vārṣṇeya</term> <gloss>Kṛṣṇa of the Vṛṣṇi clan</gloss> moved about like Time itself, destroying <term>Piśācas</term> <gloss>flesh-eating demons</gloss>, <term>Nāgas</term>, and thousands of beasts, O descendant of Bharata. It was a wondrous sight: Kṛṣṇa’s discus, the slayer of enemies, having cut down countless beings, would return to his hand again and again. While he was thus destroying the <term>Piśācas</term>, serpents, and <term>Rākṣasas</term>, the form of him who is the soul of all beings became truly terrifying. <margin>831</margin>

Of all the gods gathered there, none could emerge victorious in battle against Kṛṣṇa and the son of Pāṇḍu. When the gods could not protect their forces or extinguish that fire, they turned away. Seeing the gods retreating, <term>Śatakratu</term> felt joyful, O King, and praised <term>Keśava</term> and Arjuna. When the gods had withdrawn, a voice from the sky, deep and grave, spoke to <term>Śatakratu</term>: "Your friend, the excellent serpent <term>Takṣaka</term>, is not present here; he has gone to Kurukṣetra during this time of the burning of Khāṇḍava. <margin>832</margin> Nor can these two, <term>Vāsudeva</term> and Arjuna, be defeated in battle by any means, O <term>Vāsava</term> <gloss>Indra</gloss>. Know this from my words: they are <term>Nara</term> and <term>Nārāyaṇa</term>, the ancient gods known in heaven. You also know their power and prowess. These two, who are difficult to conquer, cannot be defeated in battle, even among all the worlds; they are the best of the ancient sages. They are most worthy of worship by all—gods, <term>Asuras</term> <gloss>demons</gloss>, <term>Yakṣas</term>, <term>Rākṣasas</term>, <term>Gandharvas</term>, humans, <term>Kinnaras</term>, and serpents. Therefore, <term>Vāsava</term>, you should depart from here with the gods. See this destruction of Khāṇḍava as something fated." <margin>833</margin> Hearing these words and realizing they were true, the lord of the immortals set aside his anger and departed for heaven.

<summary>This page recounts the climax of the burning of the Khāṇḍava forest, where Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna defeat the gods, leading to an aerial voice identifying them as the divine sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa and urging Indra to withdraw.</summary>
<keywords>Khāṇḍavadahana, Arjuna, Kṛṣṇa, Indra, Nara-Nārāyaṇa, Takṣaka, divine weapons, battle</keywords>
